title: Re-examining low-rank adaptation for private LLM fine-tuning
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Injected noise slows optimization far more than the gradient clipping alone does, so noise is the main cause of slow convergence.
layout: 1 panel, line plot with shaded confidence bands and a legend
description: A single line chart with a title reading 'RoBERTa-base on SST-2: Clip-only vs DP (95% confidence intervals, n=5 runs each)'. The x-axis is training step, from 50 to 400. The y-axis is validation loss, from about 0.25 to 0.7. An orange line with square markers shows DP-SGD. It stays flat near 0.7 until step 150, then drops steeply through step 200 and levels off near 0.32 by step 300. A wide orange confidence band opens up around step 200. A blue line with circle markers shows clipping only. It stays low, between about 0.26 and 0.31, with a narrow band. A legend in the upper right lists the means and the 95% confidence intervals. The eye goes first to the steep orange drop and the gap between the two curves.
caption: Comparison of validation loss between DP-SGD and training with per-sample clipping only (no noise added), using RoBERTa-base on SST-2 with clipping threshold C = 10. Settings follow Section 5, except that clipping-only training omits Gaussian noise. The slowdown in convergence is more pronounced for DP-SGD than for clipping alone. Lines show the mean of five runs; shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals computed from standard errors.
abstract: Privacy is a central concern when fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on sensitive data, and differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provides formal privacy guarantees. When performance at a fixed privacy level largely saturates on established benchmarks such as GLUE, we ask whether the same performance can be reached with less computation. Both theory and practice show that lower-rank models are better suited to DP training, a property especially relevant for LLMs, whose fine-tuning gradients exhibit a strong low-rank structure. Methods such as DP-LoRA exploit this by expressing each layer's weight update as a sum of only a few non-zero rank-one components. However, we argue that while having few non-zero components is important, the isotropic noise injected by DP-SGD inflates the singular values of the gradient matrix, disrupting their naturally fast decay. We investigate whether this noise-induced spectral distortion slows optimization. Experiments on language classification (GLUE with RoBERTa) and table-to-text generation (E2E and DART with Qwen and Llama models up to 4B parameters) show that partially restoring the original singular-value profile significantly accelerates DP-SGD convergence without compromising privacy guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/alidadsetan/re-exam-private-low-rank.
